summary.verdict: The page is much closer to a winner's page than it was on 12 October. It is about a fifth shorter, the results run in a clear order, and four things the first review said a Best Software judge could not find are now on it: what the three programs are, how to run the rig app, what the log contains and what licence the code carries. On validation it was already past the winners we read and it still is, with a baseline detector, a walk-forward forecast, a leave-one-arm-out table and a forecast fixed by hash. Three things hold it back now. The code has no address a judge can clone and the iGEM GitLab mirror is still a promise, which is an eligibility matter. Several sentences claim more than the result beneath them shows, such as a plate that "works as a scale-down model of the reactor" before any reactor test. And thirteen notes below are marked mistake, each quoting this page against itself or against another ReLEAF page, the cuvette path length first among them. By a rough count of the live HTML about two thirds of the words are the instructor's; the students' own sentences are mostly in R2 to R6, and that is where the praise below sits.
strengths: An argument in one sentence. "Without manual sampling, the reactor's own instruments are the only record of the batch, and they drift as they wear" sets up everything after it, and it is a student sentence.

Validation against something. R3 scores the trust layer against a plain step detector on the same data, R5 scores the Kalman filter against persistence at four horizons with a walk-forward rule stated in one line, and R6 holds out each light arm in turn. No winning software page we read compares its tool to a simpler method.
A prediction registered before the experiment, with its hash, its pass criteria in a table, and the promise that the score goes in whichever way it falls.

Measurement reporting in the newest sections. R4 gives its sites, runs, interval and 540 paired readings before any result and reports the wetness channel as untested. The silica repeat gives a protocol in one sentence and a dilute-and-restore check with SD and n at each level.

Limits placed beside the results they limit. R5 says it "forecasts the photometer reading, not biomass" directly under its table, R3 says it has been shown "on one run with one event of each kind", and the page applies its own definition to itself and calls the system a digital shadow.
priorities: Put the code where a judge can get it. Make the iGEM GitLab mirror live and print its full address in the abstract, in section 5 and in section 7. Then name the script, the log and the command behind the trust layer, so "the 434 h batch comes with it as a test case" is something a reader can run.

Settle the facts that disagree before the freeze. The cuvette is 2 mm here and on Measurement, and 0.2 mm on both Hardware pages and Contribution. Run 1's reactor readings differ between the table and the fold beside it. R2 and section 7 disagree about which instrument is the less linear. The plate-reader well is 150 µL here and 100 µL on Measurement. Fibre-break detection is unbuilt here and running on Safety. The photometer is "Calibrated" in this ledger and "uncalibrated" in Measurement's.

Narrow five claims to what was shown. The plate prior has been tested on plate arms only. Green light cost no growth, and induction has no blot behind it. "1.2 to 1.9 °C" leaves out the room site. The limit that ends "the cost is time, not yield" compares plateaus the page has no common scale for. The introduction describes in the present tense a twin that section 6 says is not yet built.

Finish the protocols. The TiO2 run still lacks its step size, its liquid, its blank and its wait. R1 lacks the hold time per pump setting. R3 never says what the score on either axis is. The photometer has a ceiling and no stated floor, on a page where two runs start near zero.

Help a judge use the software. Add a numbered walkthrough for one interface and a figure of the three parts, say who wrote the rewrite and the analysis scripts, and report whether anyone outside the dry lab has run any of it.

releaf: 5 The software that runs the reactor
winners: What it is and who needs it
Why it exists, with a number
Install: requirements, then commands, then the URL you end up with
Usage: a numbered walkthrough or a worked example
skeleton.gap: Section 5 now carries components, a run route and the log format in prose, which closes most of the gap the first review found. Three winner sections are still absent: a usage section with a numbered walkthrough, an architecture figure, and a repository line with an address. The order also differs. Winners say what the tool is and how to run it before they validate it; here four sections of results come first, so a software judge meets the software at section 5.

extras: BR-01 is never introduced. The abstract opens "BR-01 has grown B. subtilis four times" and the introduction says "Local data from BR-01". Write "our perfusion bioreactor, BR-01" at first use in each.

"This is the rig as designed." sits under a table in a section headed "What the reactor measures now". Move it above the table, as you did for the field sensors with "Today's rig software reads none of these channels."

"In the log only temperature carries its source, in temp_src; the columns are under What survives which failure." The second half points at a fold title three sections away. Write "the column list is in section 5".

"which justifies using the model as a soft sensor for flow": flow is measured by the turbine meter and tagged in-line, and the soft channels in your table are lumen ΔP, TMP and fouling ratio. The 1.03 agreement is also at one flow, with "No point was held out." Say what the model is used for and where.
"Axial non-uniformity is 28% against a 20% target": the term is never defined and the target has no source. Give each a clause.
"Past OD 1.2 the linear fit's error rises from 0.0235 to 0.1715" follows "residual SD 0.024 OD". Name the error measure, give the number of points, and use one precision for both.
"enough time for a controller to drop the faulty feed": on a perfusion reactor "feed" reads as medium. R3's last paragraph has the clearer wording: "mark OD unreliable and pause forecasts".
"flagged 23% of sensor anomalies and 0.8% of biological shifts" has no counts behind the percentages, and the table's "35–36%" is a range for a single share. Give the denominators.

"settles kLa (45.7 against 60 h⁻¹)": neither number has a source on any page, and Biomanufacturing says the culture "needs a kLa of 12.5 h−1". Say what 45.7 and 60 are estimates of. "Neither probe can be autoclaved" also needs the two probes named, because the channel table says "None fitted".

"The probe is fitted but has not been answering, so the app runs on a typed temperature." Every reactor temperature on the page, including "434 hours at 22 °C", is therefore a set value. Say so once, in the run table.
"the rig app records and the rewrite is tested on its recordings": say whether that is an automated test or a recording loaded by hand, because a judge reads "tested" as the first.

"The log is plain CSV with a fixed 73-column header" is followed by 26 column names. Write "the main columns are" and link the full header. Name run 3's nine columns too, since run 3 is the dataset you offer other teams.

The module has two geometries across our pages and the run table does not say which was fitted when. This page: "11 fibres of 1 mm bore and 0.6 m length, 0.02 m²". Hardware's bioreactor page: "Fiber area 150 cm² Fibers 8". Engineering has the reason: "The module frozen on 4 July is 150 cm² across eight fibres; the module characterised on 16 August is 200 cm² across eleven." Add the module to each run's set-up.

Figure 1's caption uses three date formats for its sources: "260610 test1 no stir.xlsx", "0721, test3 20 day.csv" and "20260902". Run 1 is also dated 6 June in the table ("prototype 260606") while its file is 260610. Keep the file names and add a note on the date.

"Valves move under software control" in the limits: the channel table has one commanded pinch valve and four Luer valves "Turned by hand; no actuator yet". Write "The pinch valve moves under software control".
"Beer–Lambert at scale." is the only limit heading that does not say what the limit is. "Linear range of the photometer" would.
"The SHT31 matched the nominal temperature of each site." Say where each nominal value comes from, so the reader knows the air probe was checked against something other than itself.
The key results row "Reads 1.2 to 1.9 °C warm against the same air; wetness untested" should follow whatever you decide for the R4 sentence about the room site.

The light array has three names across our pages. This page says "light-programmable array (LPA)"; Dry Lab Notebook says "ran them on DiOPAL in the incubator" and "the 19 September OptoLPA ACCD run". Use one name, or give the others once in brackets.

The live weather source differs from Math Model. This page: "Open-Meteo, hourly, five days back and three ahead". Math Model: "Central Weather Administration (中央氣象署) station data for live use". If these are two feeds for two jobs, say so on both pages.

Engineering still says the reference channel "flagged the window as untrustworthy while it was happening". This page now says "The alarm was computed afterwards from the log". This page has it right; ask Engineering to match.
The leaf sensor write-up links to "igem2026-leaf-sensor-bench", a repository outside iGEM's GitLab. Include it in the mirror with the rest.
References 4, 5 and 6 are never cited in the text. Cite them where they are used or remove them.

notes.anchor: so every reading here shows when it has stopped being true
notes.title: The first line promises every reading
notes.body: This is a strong opening and it claims more than the page shows. The next sentences say four results carry a second check, and only the OD channel has a reference beam; pH has no companion and the loop temperature is typed in by hand. Narrow the promise to the question the page asks of each reading.
notes.after: A reactor that runs for weeks with nobody beside it is only as good as its own record, so this page asks of each reading how we would know it had stopped being true.

notes.anchor: Both interfaces run live on this page under the MIT licence
notes.title: Say where the code is
notes.body: The licence is now in the abstract, which the first review asked for. The sheet still does not say where the code is, and Best Software eligibility needs it on iGEM's GitLab. Add the address to this sentence as soon as the mirror exists.
notes.after: Both interfaces run live on this page, and their source is at [GitLab URL] under the MIT licence.
notes.excerpt_note: UniMuenster's abstract names the platforms and how the tool is distributed, so a judge who will never install it still knows where it lives.
notes.ballot: How well is the software written and documented for future groups to extend and improve? (Code documentation, comments in the code, performance evaluation, architecture diagrams, installation and execution scripts, etc.)

notes.anchor: The loop is not closed, and almost every result rests on one run
notes.title: Two loops share one word
notes.body: Ending the abstract on its two biggest limits is the right call. On this page "the loop" is also the tubing the culture is pumped around, so a first-time reader can take this as a plumbing fault. Say which loop you mean: no decision is automated.
notes.after: No decision is automated yet: a person still makes every call about the culture. Almost every result rests on one run.

notes.anchor: 26.7 h of warning before the OD channel failed
notes.title: Nobody was warned during the run
notes.body: The paragraph above says "Replayed over the log", and R3 says "The alarm was computed afterwards from the log". This row reads as if a warning arrived in time. Many judges read only the ledger, so put the replay in the row.
notes.after: Replayed on one run's log, the alarm comes 26.7 h before the OD channel failed
notes.ballot: How well was the software validated (e.g., through experimental work, test data, or benchmarking)?

notes.anchor: 24 h biomass within 7% on held-out arms
notes.title: The held-out arms are plate arms
notes.body: The row is called Plate-to-reactor prior, and the 7% comes from holding out one light arm of the same plate. Nothing has been carried to the reactor yet; the forecast that tests that is the Pending row below. R2 also says "every OD on this page is an optical reading", so "biomass" should be OD here.
notes.after: 24 h OD within 7% on held-out arms of one plate; not yet tested on the reactor
notes.ballot: How well was the software validated (e.g., through experimental work, test data, or benchmarking)?

notes.anchor: Slope 1.018 against the BioDrop to OD 1.2, R² 0.995; both also scored against a known dose
notes.title: Calibrated here, uncalibrated on Measurement
notes.body: This row's status word is "Calibrated". Measurement's ledger describes the same instrument as "Within 3.8% of a $15,000 BioDrop, uncalibrated, R² = 0.9999" and its text says "we treat calibration as unnecessary". R2 explains the difference in a paragraph, but the two ledgers still use opposite words. Say here whether the 1.018 slope is applied to logged readings, and pick a status word both pages can use.
notes.after: Compared with the BioDrop (slope 1.018 to OD 1.2, R² 0.995) and with a known dose; the fit is [applied / not applied] to logged readings
notes.ballot: Did the team validate and calibrate their measurement process appropriately for their approach?

notes.anchor: Growth rate and shape fixed by hash before the batch
notes.title: The status word in every result row
notes.body: Your Key results ledger gives every row a one-word status: Worked, Partial, Calibrated, Bench, Pending. A judge can read the whole claim list in ten seconds and knows which rows to trust. "Pending" on a forecast that is not yet scored is the column working as it should. Keep it, and keep Partial and Bench honest when the numbers improve.
notes.excerpt_note: Vilnius counts four of five planned features shipped and names the one that did not. Your status column does the same job in one word per row.

notes.anchor: Without manual sampling, the reactor's own instruments are the only record of the batch, and they drift as they wear
notes.title: The whole page argued in one line
notes.body: This is the best sentence on the page. It gives the reader the problem (no sampling), the consequence (the instruments are the only record) and the catch (they drift) in one clause each, and everything after it is evidence for this line. Do not touch it.
notes.excerpt_note: Both winners open on the difficulty instead of the tool. Vilnius: someone had to sit with the bioreactor. William-and-Mary: soil interferes with every fluorescence method. Your sentence does the same work in half the words.

notes.anchor: the twin's trust layer flagged the reference beam 26.7 hours before the OD readings became unusable
notes.title: Say this was a replay
notes.body: Read alone, this says the trust layer warned you during the run. R3 says "The alarm was computed afterwards from the log; during the run nobody watched the trace daily and the fault was found late." The result is still a good one. Say it the way R3 does, so the introduction and the result agree.
notes.after: On the 434-hour run the OD channel failed. When we replayed the log afterwards, the twin's trust layer flagged the reference beam 26.7 hours before the OD readings became unusable.
notes.ballot: How well was the software validated (e.g., through experimental work, test data, or benchmarking)?

notes.anchor: From these it works out when to switch on green light to start protectant production, which protectant, and how much.
notes.title: Present tense for a design
notes.body: This paragraph and the one above describe the twin in the present tense. Section 2 says "Today's rig software reads none of these channels", green light is tagged planned, and your limits say every decision about the culture "still goes through a person". A judge who learns that in section 6 will reread the introduction as a claim. Say here what is designed and what runs.
notes.after: From these the twin is designed to work out when to switch on green light, which protectant to make, and how much. None of that runs yet: today's software reads only the reactor, and a person makes every decision (Gaps and limits).

notes.anchor: in-line A sensor on the loop of culture pumped around the bioreactor
notes.title: A provenance word for every value
notes.body: Tagging every channel in-line, commanded, soft, bench tested, planned or external lets a judge see at a glance which numbers are measured and which are hoped for, and you apply it in both tables. No winner we read has anything like it. The page now also says plainly that the log itself records a source for temperature only, which keeps the scheme honest.
notes.excerpt_note: Munich answers the standards question by naming formats a reader can check. Your provenance tags are the same kind of answer, and they are yours.
notes.ballot: How well is the software compatible with, and does it leverage, existing synthetic biology standards? (e.g. SBOL, other RFCs, data formats, etc.)

notes.anchor: 600 nm amber LED, 2 mm flow cuvette, sample and reference lux sensors
notes.title: Two millimetres or a fifth of one
notes.body: You give the cuvette as 2 mm here and again in sections 4 and 5, and Measurement's parts list agrees: "a 2 mm flow cuvette". Hardware's photometer page says "A 600 nm LED shines through a 0.2 mm flow cuvette", its bioreactor page says "a flow cuvette with a 0.2 mm path", and Contribution lists a "0.2 mm short optical path". The path length sits under every OD on this page. Your silica paragraph gives "a path-length factor of 5.0", which fits 2 mm scaled to 1 cm, so check the part and correct whichever pages are wrong.
notes.ballot: Did the team validate and calibrate their measurement process appropriately for their approach?

notes.anchor: Hand samples to 27 h: reactor 0.17 to 0.37, flask to 2.46
notes.title: Run one has two sets of readings
notes.body: This row has the reactor rising from 0.17 to 0.37. The fold below it says "The bioreactor stayed between 0.083 and 0.194" and "read 0.197 at 24 h", and 0.197 is outside its own band. Hardware's bioreactor page sides with the table: "from about 0.17 to 0.3–0.37 by the end of the run". Check the spreadsheet and make the table, the fold and Hardware give one set of numbers.

notes.anchor: eight pump settings from 10 to 24% in steps of 2, each measured once
notes.title: How long was each setting held
notes.body: This sentence gives the fluid, the temperature, the settings and the replicate count, and "each measured once" is exactly where a judge looks for n. Two things are missing for a team repeating it: how long each setting ran before the reading, and whether a reading is one sample or a mean over a window. Add them and R1 can be run from the page.
notes.after: 16 August 2026: water at 22 °C, eight pump settings from 10 to 24% in steps of 2, each held for [time] and read once as [one sample / the mean over a stated window], with the module fitted and again with a jumper in its place.
notes.excerpt_note: KULeuven lists every concentration, the stock and the matrix in one sentence. R1 is two facts short of that.
notes.ballot: Are the methods or protocols described well?

notes.anchor: On 23 August 2026, cumulative TiO₂ additions gave 45 paired points between the in-line photometer and the BioDrop spectrophotometer
notes.title: Half a protocol so far
notes.body: The doses and the volume are now on the page, which the first review asked for. A team repeating this still cannot get the size of each addition, the liquid the TiO₂ went into, the blank, or the wait between adding and reading. The silica paragraph below gives step, range, volume and matrix in one sentence. Write this one the same way.
notes.after: On 23 August 2026 TiO₂ was added to 500 mL of [liquid] in [mass] steps from 2 to 60 mg. After each addition the loop ran for [wait], then the in-line photometer and the BioDrop, blanked on [blank], read the same suspension. This gave 45 paired points, the last at 46 mg.
notes.excerpt_note: KULeuven's curve can be remade from one sentence: eight concentrations, the stock, the matrix and why that matrix. That is the shape your TiO2 sentence is still missing.
notes.ballot: Are the methods or protocols described well?

notes.anchor: Scoring both against the known dose, not against each other, showed that both degrade above 30 mg in different ways
notes.title: Calibrating against truth, not an instrument
notes.body: Scoring both instruments against a known dose is a better calibration design than anything in the six winning measurement pages, because it tests the reference instrument as well as yours. The clause "not against each other" is what makes it land. Keep it.
notes.excerpt_note: Austin calibrates to purchased standards and never scores the reference itself. You score both. That is the step past the winner.
notes.ballot: Did the team validate and calibrate their measurement process appropriately for their approach?

notes.anchor: while the photometer stays precise (R² 0.99, SD 0.022) and its response per milligram falls
notes.title: Which instrument stops being linear
notes.body: This sentence says the BioDrop "keeps its slope but scatters" and the photometer's "response per milligram falls". That makes the photometer the steadier one and the less linear one above 30 mg. Section 7 says the same test "showed our in-line photometer was the more linear of the two", and Measurement says "the BioDrop is slightly less linear than our own photometer". Results uses a word every page could share: "our instrument is the steadier of the two". Decide which instrument bends, then use one word everywhere.
notes.ballot: Did the team validate and calibrate their measurement process appropriately for their approach?

notes.anchor: Up to OD 1.2 the photometer regresses on the BioDrop with slope 1.018, R² 0.995, residual SD 0.024 OD
notes.title: The ceiling is defended, the floor is not
notes.body: Results gives this fit two things you leave out: "over the twenty paired points where the BioDrop reads below 1.2, the fit is ours = 1.018 × BioDrop − 0.031". Put the n and the intercept here. Then state the bottom of the range. Run 1 reads near 0.17, run 4 starts "from near zero" and the silica fit has an intercept of −0.07, so the low end is where a floor matters most.
notes.after: Over the twenty paired points where the BioDrop reads below 1.2, the photometer regresses on it with slope 1.018, intercept −0.031, R² 0.995 and residual SD 0.024 OD. Below OD [number] a reading cannot be told from the blank, whose scatter is [number].
notes.excerpt_note: Austin states OD600 0.1 as the point its plate reader stops being trustworthy. Aalto reads its curve out loud at both ends. One line each.
notes.ballot: Did the team validate and calibrate their measurement process appropriately for their approach?

notes.anchor: Measurement quotes the whole series, where both instruments fit above R² 0.999
notes.title: A note between two of our pages
notes.body: This paragraph explains to the judge why another ReLEAF page uses different numbers. Its first sentence is useful, and the result above already carries the same scope in "Over the 16 points above 30 mg". The rest is housekeeping between two teams. Fix the wording on Measurement and this paragraph can go.

notes.anchor: silica in 2.5 mg steps from 2.5 to 100 mg in 500 mL of 1% SDS, read at every step on the BioDrop
notes.title: This one is a real protocol
notes.body: Step size, range, volume, matrix, instrument, logging interval and duration, all in one sentence. A judge can repeat this. It shows you already know how to write the others.
notes.excerpt_note: This sentence is doing the same work as KULeuven's calibration passage, which is the most copyable thing on any of the six winning pages.
notes.ballot: Could the measurement(s) be reproduced by other iGEM teams?

notes.anchor: Against the reference the current build is one to one to OD 2.5 (slope 0.995, intercept −0.07)
notes.title: Name the two photometer builds
notes.body: This section says "both photometer builds", "the current build", "the 9:1 splitter build" and "the path runs 3 and 4 used", and never says what the two builds are. Hardware calls them Complex (dual beam) and Slim (single beam). "The reference" also changes meaning: here it is the BioDrop, and in the next paragraph it is the reference beam. Name each build once and say which one was fitted for runs 3 and 4.
notes.after: Against the BioDrop the dual-beam build is one to one to OD 2.5 (slope 0.995, intercept −0.07)
notes.ballot: Could the measurement(s) be reproduced by other iGEM teams?

notes.anchor: The run carries its own check. At 137.6 min the suspension was diluted and then restored
notes.title: A check that needs no known dose
notes.body: Diluting and restoring to test proportionality is clever, and the numbers are reported the way a judge wants them: three levels, each with its SD and its number of readings. Keep it, and copy the habit into R2 and R5, where the number of points behind each figure is still missing.
notes.excerpt_note: EPFL carries n, the correction and every p value in the sentence that makes the claim. Your dilution check already reads like that.
notes.ballot: Did the team validate and calibrate their measurement process appropriately for their approach?

notes.anchor: which is what the eight robust estimators are there to absorb
notes.title: Eight estimators nobody has met
notes.body: This is the only mention of "the eight robust estimators" on the page. A judge cannot tell what they estimate or why there are eight. One clause naming them, or a link to the photometer page, is enough. The finding is worth keeping: bubbles in 40% of readings and the reported value barely moves.
notes.after: One bubble flag or more appeared in 40% of readings. The photometer's eight estimators ([what they are, or a link]) are there to absorb this; between OD 3.0 and 3.2 they agree within 0.002 OD, so the choice of estimator makes little difference to the reported value.

notes.anchor: A check is an alarm when its score exceeds the 99.5th percentile of the healthy first 120 hours
notes.title: What is the score, and why these hours
notes.body: This sentence is what makes R3 a test: the threshold comes from one part of the log and is applied to the rest. Two things are missing. The page never says what the score is on either axis, so nobody can recompute it. And the first event starts at 120 h, exactly where the healthy window ends, on an alarm that was "computed afterwards from the log"; say whether 120 h was fixed before you looked at the later hours.
notes.after: Each axis is scored every 10 minutes: the sensor axis as [statistic] of the reference lux, and the process axis as [statistic] of the specific growth rate. A check is an alarm when its score exceeds the 99.5th percentile of the first 120 hours, a window we chose [before / after] seeing the rest of the log because [reason].
notes.excerpt_note: Marburg states its two pass criteria before giving the score, and says what was counted. Your threshold needs the same two things said out loud.
notes.ballot: How well was the software validated (e.g., through experimental work, test data, or benchmarking)?

notes.anchor: A standard step detector (any jump above 0.05 OD) flagged 23% of sensor anomalies and 0.8% of biological shifts
notes.title: You scored the obvious alternative
notes.body: Not one of the eight winning software pages compares its tool against a simpler method. You run the naive step detector on the same data and report that it cannot separate the two kinds of event. That one sentence is worth more than the 26.7 hours, because it says what the trust layer adds.
notes.excerpt_note: EPFL proves its material works by comparing it against water, with the test and the p values. A baseline is the cheapest validation there is, and you have one.
notes.ballot: How well was the software validated (e.g., through experimental work, test data, or benchmarking)?

notes.anchor: Four-quadrant streaks gave 168 colony morphology, which argues against a gross contaminant
notes.title: A streak from a run with no sample
notes.body: R3 opens with "no sample drawn" and the abstract repeats it. A streak plate needs culture, so one of the two statements needs a qualifier. If the streaks were made when the run ended, say so here. If they were made during the run, the 434 hours were sampled, and the headline should say how often.
notes.after: Streaks made [when] gave 168 colony morphology, which argues against a gross contaminant

notes.anchor: It has been shown on one run with one event of each kind; a detection rate needs deliberate faults on unseen batches
notes.title: You name the experiment you have not run
notes.body: This bounds the claim precisely and says what would settle it. Teams usually either overclaim or go quiet; you do neither. A judge reads this as a team that knows what its own evidence is worth.
notes.excerpt_note: EPFL says its own engineered protein cannot be confirmed statistically, then names the likely cause. Same discipline, and both teams won on it.

notes.anchor: On 10 October 2026 the field sensor rig was tested at three sites with stable air temperature
notes.title: One paragraph doing five jobs
notes.body: Opening R4 on the idea it shares with R3 was the right move. The same paragraph then carries the sites, the rig, the sensor, the method and the count of readings, in about 170 words. Break it after "sit in the same air" and start the method as its own paragraph. List the sites in the order the table uses, so the reader can match them.
notes.after: On 10 October 2026 the field sensor rig was tested at three sites: an incubator at 22 °C, a stairwell at 26.4 °C and a room at 26 °C.

notes.anchor: Each site had three five-minute runs logged every five seconds, giving 540 paired readings.
notes.title: Replicates and sampling rate, up front
notes.body: Three sites, three runs each, a sampling interval and the total, in one sentence before any result. This is the section whose n sits exactly where a judge will look for it.
notes.excerpt_note: EPFL's n and KULeuven's listed concentrations do the same job. R4 is already at winner level on this question.
notes.ballot: Could the measurement(s) be reproduced by other iGEM teams?

notes.anchor: Sharing the same air, the two sensors should agree, yet the leaf sensor read 1.2 to 1.9 °C warmer once settled
notes.title: The range leaves out the room
notes.body: Your table gives the room a site mean of +0.47 °C and a first run of −0.09, so "1.2 to 1.9" covers the incubator and the stairwell only. The words "once settled" also meet the paragraph under Figure 7, which says "Five minutes is not long enough for it to settle". The same range is repeated in the abstract, the ledger, the limits and section 7. Say which sites it comes from, or give the full spread.
notes.after: Sharing the same air, the two sensors should agree, yet the leaf sensor read 1.2 to 1.9 °C warmer in the incubator and the stairwell, and from −0.09 to +0.97 °C at the room site, where it was still climbing.
notes.ballot: Did the team validate and calibrate their measurement process appropriately for their approach?

notes.anchor: Leaf wetness read 0.0% in every sample. The sensor was never wetted
notes.title: A channel reported as untested
notes.body: Reporting a flat zero and then saying the test cannot show whether the channel responds is harder to write than it looks. Most teams would have called 0.0% a dry reading and moved on. Keep both sentences; they are the ones a measurement judge will believe you on.
notes.excerpt_note: Aalto reports a whole measurement as below the detection limit and excludes it from the arithmetic. Yours is the same refusal to let a number stand for more than it shows.
notes.ballot: Did the team validate and calibrate their measurement process appropriately for their approach?

notes.anchor: We compared Kalman filter, local linear, global linear and exponential forecasts against persistence, which predicts no change.
notes.title: Five models in, two in the table
notes.body: You compare five forecasts and the table reports two. A judge who wants to know whether the Kalman filter beats local linear has to read it off Figure 8. The table also needs its unit and its n: RMSE in OD, over how many hourly forecasts at each horizon. The tab label says "rules fixed in advance"; one clause on which rules were fixed, and when, would back that up.
notes.after: At 2 h ahead the errors were persistence 0.067, Kalman 0.040, local linear [RMSE], global linear [RMSE] and exponential [RMSE], in OD, over [n] hourly forecasts.
notes.ballot: How well was the software validated (e.g., through experimental work, test data, or benchmarking)?

notes.anchor: A forecast was made every hour from 12 h, each using only data up to that point.
notes.title: Walk-forward stated in one line
notes.body: This sentence is what stops a reader asking whether the filter saw the future. It is one short line, and it makes the whole table believable. Judges look for exactly this clause and usually do not find it.
notes.ballot: How well was the software validated (e.g., through experimental work, test data, or benchmarking)?

notes.anchor: The 12-hour median OD rose from 1.06 to 3.75, so R5 forecasts the photometer reading, not biomass.
notes.title: The limit sits beside the result
notes.body: The first review asked for this caveat to move up from the limits list, and here it is, directly under the table. You say what the forecast is a forecast of, and your next sentence says what survives: the comparison holds because every model sees the same signal. A judge trusts the 41% more for it.
notes.excerpt_note: KULeuven says what OD600 cannot distinguish in the section that uses the reading. You now do the same.
notes.ballot: How well was the software validated (e.g., through experimental work, test data, or benchmarking)?

notes.anchor: A logistic model beat logistic-with-lag by AICc
notes.title: One sentence carrying six numbers
notes.body: This sentence holds the model choice, a gloss of AICc, the fit error, a gloss of NRMSE, R², the criterion and three parameters. Each is worth having, and together they are hard to read. Split it into the choice, the fit and the parameters. K and X0 also need their scale, which is plate-reader OD.
notes.after: A logistic model beat logistic-with-lag by AICc, a score that penalises the extra parameter. It fits at NRMSE 1.9% (normalised root-mean-square error; R² 0.997), against the 15% criterion for bioprocess models [3]. The fitted values are r = 0.299 ± 0.017 h⁻¹ (doubling time 139 min), K = 1.005 and X0 = 0.0235, the last two in plate-reader OD.

notes.anchor: Across these six light arms, green induction costs no growth
notes.title: Green light, yes; induction, not shown
notes.body: The data show that green light cost no growth. Whether the green arms were induced is a separate claim, and Measurement says of the Western blot from these samples: "Neither scan in the draft carries a readable band, so neither is reproduced here and no expression claim rests on them." Until a blot shows expression, write light where you now write induction.
notes.after: Across these six light arms, green light costs no growth: r spans 0.279 to 0.317 h⁻¹, within one standard error, and the weakest-green arm reaches the highest plateau. Whether the green arms were induced is not shown, because the Western blot from these samples has no readable band (Measurement).

notes.anchor: we left out each arm in turn, fitted the other five, and predicted its 24 h OD from its first 8 hours
notes.title: Leave-one-out, with the table to prove it
notes.body: Not one of the fourteen winning pages we read holds data back from its own fit. You do, you give all six arms, and you give the prediction with and without the prior side by side so the reader can see what the prior buys. This is the strongest single piece of evidence on the page.
notes.excerpt_note: Marburg's structure benchmark is the closest any winner comes, and it has no held-out set and no comparison condition. Yours has both.
notes.ballot: How well was the software validated (e.g., through experimental work, test data, or benchmarking)?

notes.anchor: Observed OD at 24 h
notes.title: What the observed column contains
notes.body: Measurement's table for this run gives the red arms at 24 h as "1.026, 0.969, 1.026" with a blank of 0.059, so your 0.967, 0.910 and 0.967 are blank-subtracted. Measurement also says each green arm is three tubes and each red arm is one, and that the culture is "WB800 + CcaSR". None of that is on this page, and neither is the model behind "Without the prior". Put all four in a line under the table.
notes.after: Observed values are the 24 h readings on Measurement minus the 0.059 blank. Each green value is the mean of three tubes and each red value is one tube, all of WB800 carrying CcaS/CcaR. "Without the prior" is [the model fitted to that arm's own readings to 8 h].
notes.ballot: Could the measurement(s) be reproduced by other iGEM teams?

notes.anchor: The plate works as a scale-down model of the reactor, as in biomanufacturing process transfer [3].
notes.title: The reactor has not been tested yet
notes.body: The leave-one-arm-out test shows the prior predicts an unseen arm of the same plate. It does not show that the plate predicts the reactor. Section 4 says the forecast that tests this "has not been scored yet", and your June fold reports the stirred reactor growing at four times the plate rate. State what was shown and point at the test.
notes.after: On the plate, the prior predicts an arm it has not seen. Whether it predicts the reactor is what the registered forecast in section 4 tests.
notes.ballot: How well was the software validated (e.g., through experimental work, test data, or benchmarking)?

notes.anchor: To test the twin's forecast, we registered it before a reactor run of B. subtilis WB800 with constitutive ACC deaminase secretion
notes.title: Nobody else in this prize does this
notes.body: A forecast fixed by hash before the run, with its pass criteria in a table and the promise that the score goes in whichever way it falls. None of the eight Best Software winners and none of the six Best Measurement winners we read registered a prediction. Keep the hash, keep the table, and keep the promise.
notes.excerpt_note: Marburg states its pass criteria before the score, which is the closest any winner comes. You state yours before the experiment.
notes.ballot: How well was the software validated (e.g., through experimental work, test data, or benchmarking)?

notes.anchor: The forecast file is prereg_forecast_20261002.json
notes.title: Let the reader check the hash
notes.body: A registered forecast is as strong as the reader's ability to check it. The page prints the hash with its middle cut out, gives no date in words, and does not link the file, which sits in software/figures/ beside the figure script. Print the whole hash, the date, and the commit that first carried the file.
notes.after: The forecast file is software/figures/prereg_forecast_20261002.json, registered on [date] in commit [id]. Its SHA-256 is [all 64 characters].
notes.ballot: How well was the software validated (e.g., through experimental work, test data, or benchmarking)?

notes.anchor: Why only the growth rate is scored
notes.title: Three criteria or one
notes.body: This fold says "only r is scored", and R6 says "the registered forecast predicts r alone". The table directly above lists three predictions, each with a pass criterion: growth rate, curve shape and time to reach OD 0.5. A time to reach OD 0.5 also depends on the OD scale, which this fold says has no cross-calibration yet. Say which rows will be scored and on which scale, or take two rows out.
notes.ballot: How well was the software validated (e.g., through experimental work, test data, or benchmarking)?

notes.anchor: were fitted on the plate-reader scale in a 150 µL well
notes.title: The well volume differs from Measurement
notes.body: You give the plate-reader well as 150 µL. Measurement's procedure for the same run says: "From each of the 12 tubes take 200 µL: 100 µL for OD600 and 100 µL for Western blot." The volume sets the depth of liquid the plate reader looks through, so it matters to the cross-calibration this fold is about. Check the notebook and make both pages agree.
notes.ballot: Could the measurement(s) be reproduced by other iGEM teams?

notes.anchor: It is the Arduino App Lab application our instructor Chars Hsieh wrote for the Uno Q board on BR-01
notes.title: Who wrote the other pieces
notes.body: Naming the author of the rig app is honest, and a judge will respect it. The page then stops: it does not say who wrote the rewrite, the trust layer, the forecasts or the figure scripts. A Best Software judge is scoring the team's software, so this is one of the first things they will want to know. One sentence here answers it.
notes.after: It is the Arduino App Lab application our instructor Chars Hsieh wrote for the Uno Q board on BR-01, and it recorded every reactor number on this page. The rewrite was written by [name], and the trust layer, the forecasts and the figure scripts by [names].

notes.anchor: It has three parts. Firmware v3.10.9 (sketch/sketch.ino) runs on the Uno Q's microcontroller
notes.title: Draw these three boxes
notes.body: This paragraph is what the first review asked for: each part has a file, a place it runs and a job, and the last sentence says how they talk. The ballot names architecture diagrams, and the rig app's README already has one drawn in text characters. Redraw it as a figure here: three boxes, the Bridge link between two of them, and port 7000 out to the browser.
notes.excerpt_note: Vilnius gives every component its name, its technology and a verb. Your paragraph now does the same, so the figure only has to repeat it.
notes.ballot: How well is the software written and documented for future groups to extend and improve? (Code documentation, comments in the code, performance evaluation, architecture diagrams, installation and execution scripts, etc.)

notes.anchor: The source is in software/rig-app/, with a README in Traditional Chinese.
notes.title: A path needs a repository
notes.body: The run route is new and it is concrete: one library with its version, one brick, one address. Two gaps remain. "software/rig-app/" is a path inside a repository the page never names, so a reader cannot clone it. And the only README is in Traditional Chinese, so for an English-reading judge this paragraph is the whole manual; say that, and treat it as the English summary.
notes.after: The source is in software/rig-app/ of [repository URL]. Its README is in Traditional Chinese, and the steps below are the English summary.
notes.excerpt_note: UniMuenster tested its install guide on two operating systems and on a team member with no command-line experience, and says so. A route is only documentation once someone else has followed it.
notes.ballot: How well is the software written and documented for future groups to extend and improve? (Code documentation, comments in the code, performance evaluation, architecture diagrams, installation and execution scripts, etc.)

notes.anchor: Six tabs: what to do now, a live P&ID, the growth twin against its forecast band, weather and blast risk, the batch record, and setup.
notes.title: Six tab names are not a walkthrough
notes.body: Both interfaces run on the page, which is more than most winners offer. Neither has a walkthrough, so a judge opens the embed and has to guess where to click. Pick one task and number the steps. Write P&ID out as well: piping and instrumentation diagram.
notes.after: A first look takes three steps. 1. Open the page full screen; with no board attached it runs on simulated data. 2. Open [tab] and read [what it shows]. 3. Open [tab] and [what to try].
notes.excerpt_note: INSA Lyon hands the reader its own experiment as a worked example, with every value to type in. Three numbered steps on your own simulated data would do the same.
notes.ballot: Is the software user-friendly?

notes.anchor: At 22 °C growth is 28 times slower but plateaus at OD 1.454, within noise of the 37 °C plateau
notes.title: A comparison the page cannot make
notes.body: No growth rate at 22 °C appears anywhere on the page, so "28 times slower" has nothing to be checked against. No 37 °C run here plateaus near 1.454 either: run 2 held 0.84, the plate's K is 1.005 on the plate-reader scale, and run 4's temperature is not given. The reading is also above the OD 1.2 limit of the path it was taken on. Give the two rates and name the 37 °C plateau, or drop "the cost is time, not yield".
notes.after: At 22 °C growth is 28 times slower ([rate] against [rate] h⁻¹ in [which run]) and plateaus at OD 1.454 on the in-line scale. That reading is above the OD 1.2 limit of its path, so we cannot yet say whether the plateau matches 37 °C.

notes.anchor: Any team with an optical sensor can use it; the 434 h batch comes with it as a test case.
notes.title: Comes with it, from where
notes.body: This is the page's best reuse offer and the reader cannot take it up. No file, script or command is named, and nobody outside the team is reported to have tried any of the seven items in this list. Name the script and the log, give the command that redraws Figure 4, and if another team or a classmate has run it, say who.
notes.after: Any team with an optical sensor and a reference channel can use it. The script is [path], the 434 h log is [path], and [command] reproduces Figure 4 and the alarm at 216.3 h.
notes.excerpt_note: INSA Lyon gives the dataset and every parameter so a reader can rerun the team's own result. Fudan names two teams that used its tool. Those are the two strong kinds of reuse evidence.
notes.ballot: Can the software be useful to other projects?

notes.anchor: The board sends PV OD=0.412 PH=7.02 FLOW=263 PT1=2.69 PT3=1.31 PT4=0.45 PT5=0.35.
notes.title: Fields without units or names
notes.body: Showing the two lines is what the integration question asks for, and the heartbeat and timeout are explained well. The example still needs a key. It carries four PT fields while section 2 says the firmware reads three pressure transducers, and no field has a unit; if PT1 is in bar, 2.69 is above your 0.5 bar interlock. Add one line that names each field and its unit.
notes.after: Fields: OD in [unit], PH, FLOW in [unit], and PT1, PT3, PT4 and PT5, which are [the transducer each one is] in [unit].
notes.excerpt_note: Vilnius says exactly how the hardware and the server talk, component by component. Your two lines are the same idea and need only their labels.
notes.ballot: How well can the software be integrated with external tools/software applications? (APIs, packages, etc.)

notes.anchor: A broken fibre shows up as a trans-membrane pressure anomaly, and those transducers are already logged, so detection is a software change.
notes.title: Three versions of fibre-break detection
notes.body: Here detection is "a software change", so it is not built. Your own limits say "Trans-membrane pressure is below transducer resolution at the operating point", and that is the signal this bullet relies on. Safety describes it as running: "Real-time monitoring of transmembrane pressure ensures early detection of membrane integrity failure". Agree one sentence with the Safety authors and use it on both pages.
notes.after: A broken fibre should change the pressures across the membrane, and those transducers are already logged. We have not tested this: trans-membrane pressure is below transducer resolution at the operating point.

notes.anchor: all of it will be mirrored to gitlab.igem.org/2026/software-tools/ before the wiki freeze
notes.title: The eligibility line is in future tense
notes.body: Best Software has two entry conditions: an OSI-approved licence, and source code "hosted on the dedicated repository in iGEM's GitLab". The licence is done. This sentence is the other condition, and it is a promise with an address that has no team name in it, beside a "team repository" the page never links. When the mirror exists, replace the promise with the link.
notes.after: The rig app, the rewrite, the figure scripts and the numbers behind them are at [full GitLab URL], under the MIT licence.
notes.ballot: How well is the software written and documented for future groups to extend and improve? (Code documentation, comments in the code, performance evaluation, architecture diagrams, installation and execution scripts, etc.)

resolved.anchor: No result rests on one instrument
resolved.title: This claim is wider than the page
resolved.body: Your own last sentence says "almost every result rests on one run", and R5 rests on one plate reader while R4's forecast rests on the photometer alone. Three of the seven rows below have a single instrument behind them. Narrow the claim to the results that really carry a cross-check.
resolved.after: Four results carry a second, independent check:

resolved.anchor: a reference beam that never sees the culture separates lamp drift from growth
resolved.title: Four cross-checks in one sentence
resolved.body: This sentence runs for about seventy words and lists four different cross-checks before the reader has met any of them. It is the second thing a judge reads. Give the principle its own short sentence and let the four checks follow as a list.
resolved.after: No result rests on one instrument. A reference beam that never sees the culture separates lamp drift from growth. Wall shear is computed twice, from pressure and from flow. The photometer is scored against a known TiO₂ dose. The field leaf sensor is scored against an air probe in the same air.

resolved.anchor: the photometer was calibrated against a known TiO₂ dose
resolved.title: Our two pages disagree about calibration
resolved.body: This page says the photometer "was calibrated against a known TiO₂ dose". Our Measurement page says the opposite about the same instrument: "Our central contribution is a validated, calibration-free in-line OD600 measurement device" and "Therefore, we treat calibration as unnecessary." A measurement judge who opens both pages sees one experiment reported two ways. Agree on one account with the Measurement team and write it in the same words on both pages.
resolved.after: the photometer was scored against a known TiO₂ dose
resolved.ballot: Did the team validate and calibrate their measurement process appropriately for their approach?

resolved.anchor: That layer gave 26.7 hours of warning before the OD channel failed
resolved.title: Which layer is that layer
resolved.body: The sentence before this one names four separate cross-checks, so "that layer" has nothing single to point back to. Name the trust layer, and say the warning came from one event on one run, which is what your limits already admit.
resolved.after: The trust layer gave 26.7 hours of warning before the OD channel failed, on one event in one 434-hour run.
resolved.excerpt_note: EPFL attaches n to the headline number itself, so the reader never has to look for it.
resolved.ballot: Could the measurement(s) be reproduced by other iGEM teams?

resolved.anchor: Slope 1.018 against BioDrop, R² 0.995, on a known dose
resolved.title: Two different scorings in one row
resolved.body: The slope of 1.018 and R² 0.995 come from regressing the photometer on the BioDrop up to OD 1.2. The known-dose scoring is a separate analysis with different numbers. This row reads as though one fit did both. Pick the number you want in the headline and say what it was measured against.
resolved.after: Slope 1.018 against the BioDrop to OD 1.2, R² 0.995; both instruments also scored against a known dose
resolved.ballot: Did the team validate and calibrate their measurement process appropriately for their approach?

resolved.anchor: Nobody will be there to take samples or read every value, so the digital twin makes the decisions
resolved.title: The page later says a person decides
resolved.body: Your Current limits say the opposite: "every decision about the culture, above all induction, still goes through a person", and the abstract says "The loop is not closed." A judge will read this opening sentence as a claim the rest of the page withdraws. Put it in the tense you mean.
resolved.after: Nobody will be there to take samples or read every value, so the twin has to turn the instrument readings into a recommendation a farmer can act on.

resolved.anchor: The twin also decides when to switch on green light to start protectant production, which protectant, and how much
resolved.title: One paragraph doing five jobs
resolved.body: This paragraph covers regional data, field sensors, local data, the induction rule, the forecast, the prior and a future assay. The reader cannot hold it. Split it in two: what the twin reads, then what it decides from it.
resolved.after:
The twin reads three kinds of data. Regional data (the weather forecast, crop-stress risk and the Geospatial Analysis maps) show when and where crops will come under stress. Field sensors beside the crop measure leaf temperature, leaf wetness, and air temperature and humidity (R6). Local data from BR-01 show how much biomass is in the loop and whether those readings can be trusted (R3).

From these it decides when to switch on green light, which protectant and how much. Induction makes sense when the field is heading into stress and the culture can respond, and the forecast (R4) and growth prior (R5) say whether the batch will be ready in time.

resolved.anchor: Photometer: amber LED, 2 mm flow cuvette, sample and reference lux sensors
resolved.title: Say the wavelength, not the colour
resolved.body: "Amber" is a colour; OD600 is a wavelength claim. Our Hardware photometer page gives the number and ties the two together: "600 nm sits in a strong amber, right in the middle of the green (~535 nm) and red (~672 nm) peaks of CcaS". Put the number here, because a judge checking whether your OD600 is really an OD600 looks at this row.
resolved.after: Photometer: 600 nm amber LED, 2 mm flow cuvette, sample and reference lux sensors
resolved.ballot: Did the team validate and calibrate their measurement process appropriately for their approach?

resolved.anchor: Today's rig software reads none of these.
resolved.title: A fact that lands before its subject
resolved.body: "These" has no referent yet; the table comes after this sentence. Let the reader see the channels first, then tell them nothing reads them.
resolved.after: These are the channels outside the reactor: what the plants are experiencing, and what the weather is about to do. Today's rig software reads none of them. They belong to the next interface, and the leaf and air sensors have been on a bench but never on a plant (R6).

resolved.anchor: The interface applies the BLASTAM rule for leaf blast [7]: a wet period counts when the leaf stays wet 10 h at 22–25 °C
resolved.title: Six thresholds for a rule that fires nothing
resolved.body: This fold spends a hundred words and three references on the exact hour-and-temperature table for a rule that your last sentence says "triggers nothing". Keep why the rule is there and the fact that it is unscored, and move the threshold table to wherever the rule is implemented.
resolved.after: The interface applies the BLASTAM rule for leaf blast [7], which counts a wet period from leaf wetness hours and temperature, using the sensor for past hours and forecast humidity for future ones [8, 9]. The sensor is still on a bench, the rule is unscored on Taiwanese fields, and ACC deaminase is untested against blast, so blast risk is shown to the grower and triggers nothing.

resolved.anchor: BR-01 has grown B. subtilis five times. Runs 1 and 2 were June prototypes sampled by hand against a shake flask
resolved.title: The abstract already said this
resolved.body: "BR-01 has grown B. subtilis five times" opens the abstract word for word. The chapter eyebrow above already says "Five runs". Start on the thing the abstract did not say.
resolved.after: Runs 1 and 2 were June prototypes sampled by hand against a shake flask; from July the in-line photometer took over. Figure 1 shows the four finished runs.

resolved.anchor: 16 August 2026: water at 22 °C, eight pump settings, once with the module fitted and once with a jumper in its place
resolved.title: Say how many times each setting was read
resolved.body: You give the date, the fluid, the temperature and the eight settings, which is most of a protocol. The one thing a team repeating this needs and cannot get is how many readings you took at each setting and how long you waited for the pressure to settle. Both are in your log.
resolved.after: 16 August 2026: water at 22 °C, eight pump settings, each held [number] s and read [number] times, once with the module fitted and once with a jumper in its place.
resolved.excerpt_note: KULeuven lists every standard concentration and the matrix they were made in, so the curve can be remade. One line of that kind here fixes R1 for both measurement questions.
resolved.ballot: Are the methods or protocols described well?

resolved.anchor: The 25 August progress report gives 0.084 bar and 0.90–0.96× theory for the same measurement
resolved.title: Two unresolved notes left in public
resolved.body: The page now carries two folds called "To reconcile before the freeze", this one and the one in R2. Each tells a judge that we have two answers for one measurement and have not chosen. In both cases you have chosen: here the next sentence says the figures are the later analysis, and in R2 the scoped figure is the right one. Put the decision in the body as a reason, and keep a fold only for what is still genuinely open.
resolved.after: Both figures come from one spreadsheet; the 0.096 bar and 1.03× quoted here are from the later re-analysis, which corrected [what changed]. The 25 August progress report's 0.084 bar and 0.90–0.96× are superseded.

resolved.anchor: Wall shear can be computed from the pressure drop or from the flow rate, and the two agree to 2.8%
resolved.title: Our notebook says ten per cent
resolved.body: Our Dry Lab Notebook reports the same cross-check from the same measurement as agreeing "to within 10 per cent". The whole argument in section 5 is that October's 20% disagreement is a fault because August agreed to 2.8%. At 10% it is much less of an outlier. Settle which number is right before the freeze, because this one sentence carries the clogging indicator.
resolved.ballot: How well was the software validated (e.g., through experimental work, test data, or benchmarking)?

resolved.anchor: B. subtilis 168 growth log with the photometer
resolved.title: The heading hides the result
resolved.body: Your contents rail calls this R3 Trust layer, and the section's finding is that the trust layer caught a failing instrument. This heading names the dataset instead. Give the heading the finding.
resolved.after: The trust layer on a 434-hour growth log

resolved.anchor: 21 July to 8 August 2026: 434 hours of B. subtilis 168 at 22 °C, 2,671 valid rows, no sample drawn
resolved.title: Our Hardware pages name a different strain
resolved.body: You say 168. Our Hardware bioreactor page says of the same run: "A continuous run of engineered B. subtilis WB800 at 22 °C, drawn from the bioreactor loop", and Hardware photometer and Engineering say WB800 too. Results and Biomanufacturing back you ("Every reactor number on this wiki is strain 168, run 4 included"). Five pages, two strains, one run. Fix this first: it decides whether the page's main dataset is a wild-type or an engineered culture.
resolved.ballot: Could the measurement(s) be reproduced by other iGEM teams?

resolved.anchor: Contamination found no support; the culture still smelled of B. subtilis and four-quadrant streaks gave 168 morphology
resolved.title: Say what each check ruled out
resolved.body: Two checks are named and neither says what it excludes. A smell test and a streak plate rule out different things, and a judge grading controls needs the clause. Smell is also not a method a reader can repeat without knowing what you were comparing it to.
resolved.after: Contamination found no support. Four-quadrant streaks gave 168 colony morphology with no second morphology, which rules out a gross bacterial contaminant; the culture also still had the characteristic B. subtilis odour, which is weaker evidence and is reported as such.
resolved.excerpt_note: William-and-Mary gives each control a rule attached to it: a negative control with plaques voids the whole session. One clause per control is enough.
resolved.ballot: Did the team validate and calibrate their measurement process appropriately for their approach?

resolved.anchor: On the 434-hour run this gave 26.7 hours to mark OD unreliable and pause forecasts while the readings still looked normal
resolved.title: Put the n where the number is
resolved.body: The honest bound is in the next sentence, which is the right thing to have written. Move the scope into the sentence that makes the claim, so a judge skimming the section cannot take 26.7 hours as a capability.
resolved.after: On this one run, with one instrument event, the trust layer gave 26.7 hours to mark OD unreliable and pause forecasts while the readings still looked normal.
resolved.excerpt_note: EPFL never states a result without its n in the same sentence. It costs four words and it closes the question a judge would otherwise ask.
resolved.ballot: Could the measurement(s) be reproduced by other iGEM teams?

resolved.anchor: Global linear and exponential fits did worse than persistence at short horizons.
resolved.title: The fold below says this better
resolved.body: The fold directly under this sentence explains why global linear and exponential fall behind, in more detail and more clearly. Keeping both means the reader meets the same fact twice in twenty words.
resolved.after: A two-state Kalman filter (level and slope) beats persistence at every horizon, by less as the horizon grows.

resolved.anchor: grew in light-programmable array wells under six light arms, read on a plate reader at five time points to 24 h
resolved.title: Our plate map has one red intensity
resolved.body: Your six arms are weak, medium and high red and the same three greens. Our Measurement page's plate map for this run says: "red at 168 lux in columns 1, 3 and 5, and green at 220, 510 and 3850 lux in columns 2, 4 and 6". If all three red columns sat at 168 lux, then R1, R2 and R3 are replicates of one condition and not three light levels, which changes what leaving one out tests.
resolved.ballot: Did the team validate and calibrate their measurement process appropriately for their approach?

resolved.anchor: A logistic model beat logistic-with-lag by AICc and fits at NRMSE 1.9%
resolved.title: AICc and NRMSE, both unexplained
resolved.body: Two model-selection terms in one clause, neither expanded, in the first sentence of the section. A judge from outside modelling stops reading here. Six words of gloss keeps them.
resolved.after: A logistic model fitted the data better than a logistic model with a lag phase, by AICc, which penalises the extra parameter. It fits at 1.9% normalised root-mean-square error (R² 0.997), against the 15% criterion for bioprocess models [3]

resolved.anchor: Green induction costs no growth: r spans 0.279 to 0.317 h⁻¹ across the six arms, within one standard error
resolved.title: A strong claim, bounded two folds later
resolved.body: This reads as a general finding about green light, and the fold below says the six arms are near-identical so the test cannot speak to a new condition. The bound belongs in the same breath as the claim.
resolved.after: Across these six light arms, green induction costs no growth: r spans 0.279 to 0.317 h⁻¹, within one standard error, and the highest-green arm reaches the highest plateau. The arms are biologically near-identical, so this is a reproducibility result and not a test of a new condition.

resolved.anchor: A reactor run takes days; a plate run takes 24 hours and tests six conditions.
resolved.title: The reason for this test arrives last
resolved.body: This is why the plate prior exists, and it sits in the closing paragraph after the whole experiment. Move it to the top of the section so the reader knows what the test is for before reading the table.
resolved.after: A reactor run takes days; a plate run takes 24 hours and tests six conditions, so a prior fitted on a plate would let the twin forecast from the first few hours, when R4's Kalman filter has least to work with. On 19 September 2026, B. subtilis WB800 grew in light-programmable array wells...
resolved.excerpt_note: Vilnius puts the reason the tool exists in sentence two. The casebook's commonest fault among winners is that reason arriving late.

resolved.anchor: the gap opened from −0.42 °C at the start of run 1 to +1.11 °C at the end of run 3
resolved.title: These are not the run means
resolved.body: The table two paragraphs above gives the room's three runs as −0.09, +0.54 and +0.97. These two numbers are the first and last readings inside the runs, which is a different thing, and nothing says so. A reader checking the table against this sentence finds four numbers that do not match.
resolved.after: the gap opened from −0.42 °C in the first readings of run 1 to +1.11 °C in the last readings of run 3, against run means of −0.09, +0.54 and +0.97

resolved.anchor: That leaves two readings of the same data, and this test cannot separate them
resolved.title: The same alternative, told twice
resolved.body: Your Must-have table says this already: "separates a site-dependent bias from an unfinished warm-up". Two full sentences here and a table row there is one too many. Keep the short version here and let the table carry the fix.
resolved.after: Five minutes is not long enough for it to settle, so this test cannot tell a site-dependent offset from a sensor still warming from cold. Deciding between them needs a logged start time and a longer run.

resolved.anchor: The LPA run's temperature was not recorded
resolved.title: Our own protocol gives the plate a temperature
resolved.body: Our Measurement page's LPA procedure says "Prewarm the media to 37 °C" and "Start the light program, incubate at 37 °C, shaking, for 8 to 10 hours total." This sentence is the reason the registered forecast excuses itself from a 37 °C reactor batch. If the plate also ran at 37 °C, that reason disappears and the criterion applies after all. Check the incubator setting and rewrite this clause either way.
resolved.ballot: How well was the software validated (e.g., through experimental work, test data, or benchmarking)?

resolved.anchor: The same batch carries the first ACC deaminase activity assay
resolved.title: An earlier activity assay already exists
resolved.body: Our Math Model page reports "DNPH ACC deaminase activity assay, 2026-10-07, 7.2514 mU mL⁻¹ supernatant", and Development describes the same measurement. That is the day before this batch, so this is not the first. Measurement also says the readout had to be Berthelot ammonium because DNPH was unavailable, while your criterion is written in α-ketobutyrate. Say which assay and which readout you mean.
resolved.after: The same batch carries the first ACC deaminase activity assay run on reactor permeate, with its bar set in advance

resolved.anchor: ELISA follows on the CcaS/CcaR version once the western blot band is strong enough.
resolved.title: The assay plan belongs on Measurement
resolved.body: This fold is the only wet-lab assay on a software page, it has no result yet, and it ends in a plan for a second assay that depends on a third. Keep the one line that ties the assay to this batch and send the rest to Measurement, which the page already points to.
resolved.after: The same batch carries the first ACC deaminase activity assay, with its bar set in advance: at least 1 mU/mL in cell-free permeate, n = 3, against an empty-vector permeate and a minus-ACC blank. The assay and its follow-ups are on Measurement.

resolved.anchor: One file, no install, served by the board on port 7000 in English or Traditional Chinese
resolved.title: No route for a judge to the code
resolved.body: This describes the farmer's experience, not a reader's. There is no clone URL, no dependency list, no command and nothing a judge can open on their own machine, and the Best Software rules make an open-source repository in iGEM's GitLab an eligibility item. Five of the eight winners print the clone URL and the command in the body. You have a versioned zip, a README and a licence; print them here.
resolved.after: One file, no install, served by the board on port 7000 in English or Traditional Chinese, with an explanation and normal range behind every information mark. The source is at [repository URL] under the MIT licence; clone it and copy the sketch to an Uno Q board, or open [file] in a browser to see the interface against recorded data with no board attached.
resolved.excerpt_note: INSAENSLyon1 writes its install section for a biologist who has never opened a terminal. UniMuenster says in the abstract which platforms it runs on and how it is distributed. Both are a paragraph each.
resolved.ballot: How well is the software written and documented for future groups to extend and improve? (Code documentation, comments in the code, performance evaluation, architecture diagrams, installation and execution scripts, etc.)

resolved.anchor: Derived against the provisional baseline: wall shear 4996 s⁻¹, ΔP ratio 0.83, γ ratio 1.01
resolved.title: Three terms the reader has not met
resolved.body: ΔP ratio and γ ratio appear here for the first time and are only defined two folds later, and "the provisional baseline" is explained in section 6. The paragraph that follows is about these two numbers disagreeing, so the reader needs them first.
resolved.after: Derived: wall shear 4996 s⁻¹, and two clogging indicators, the ΔP ratio at 0.83 and the γ ratio at 1.01. Both divide today's reading by a clean-module baseline that has not been re-measured on this plumbing, so both are marked provisional.

resolved.anchor: The rig app's interlocks, board-side recording, bubble rejection and calibration bookkeeping each exist because a run failed without them
resolved.title: Your best argument is the last line
resolved.body: This sentence explains why the whole section exists, and it is at the bottom of the page's second-longest section. No winning page has a sentence like it. Open section 5 with it.
resolved.after: Every feature in the rig app is there because a run failed without it: the interlocks, the board-side recording, the bubble rejection and the calibration bookkeeping. Every number on this page was recorded by that one program, the Arduino App Lab application our instructor Chars wrote for the Uno Q board on BR-01.
resolved.excerpt_note: Marburg opens on its own measured failure, 27% of combinations active, and the tool arrives as the answer to it. Same structure, and yours covers four features at once.

resolved.anchor: That makes it a digital shadow with actuation [1, 2].
resolved.title: The page is titled Digital Twin
resolved.body: Your own fold in section 1 defines a shadow as a system where changes back still need a person, and a twin as one where they do not. This bullet says the project is the first. A judge who has read both will want the page to say so near the top, not in the eighth limit. Being a shadow and saying so is a stronger position than a twin claim the page withdraws.
resolved.after: The loop is not closed. Valves move under software control, but every decision about the culture, above all induction, still goes through a person, so by the definition in section 1 this is a digital shadow with actuation and not yet a twin [1, 2].

resolved.anchor: A documented two-line ASCII protocol with a heartbeat watchdog, interlocks on the microcontroller
resolved.title: The protocol is named, never shown
resolved.body: This is the only mention of the protocol and the harness on the page, and it is a bullet in the last section. A judge grading integration wants two lines of it: one command out, one reply in. You say it is documented, so the lines exist. Show them, and say what the harness covers and the command that runs it.
resolved.after: The serial protocol and test harness. Two ASCII lines carry everything: the board sends `D,1738.2,0.1758,6.500,...` once a window, and the page sends `C,pump,145` back, with a heartbeat that latches a fault if either side goes quiet for [number] ms. The desktop harness replays a recorded log against the page and the firmware with no board attached, and runs with [command].
resolved.excerpt_note: Vilnius publishes its API spec as a file; Munich prints curl calls. The route in and the route out, written as something you could type, is what this ballot question rewards.
resolved.ballot: How well can the software be integrated with external tools/software applications? (APIs, packages, etc.)

resolved.anchor: The pressure logging also gives the project's cheapest biocontainment layer.
resolved.title: This fold belongs on Safety
resolved.body: The page already points at Safety for the other three containment layers, and this fold argues a safety case in a section about what other teams can reuse. The reusable part is one clause: pressure transducers you already log will show a broken fibre.
resolved.after: (keep one line in the For other teams list: "Pressure logging as containment monitoring. A broken fibre shows up as a trans-membrane pressure anomaly, and those transducers are already logged, so detection is a software change. The other three layers are on Safety.")
